title: Extraction of Microplastics from Solid Biowastes for µ-FTIR Analysis
author: Ruffell, Pantos, et al.

steps.title: Weigh and spike samples
steps.instruction: Weigh 30 g of each dried biowaste (biosolids, compost, soil) directly into a pre‑cleaned 600 mL glass beaker, cover with aluminium foil, and perform the procedure in triplicate for each sample type plus a reagent‑only control. Spike each sample with one fragment (500–1000 µm) of each polymer (PET, PVC, HIPS, PP, ABS, HDPE, PA) and ten pieces each of PE microbeads and PMMA fibres.

steps.title: Prepare Fe(II) solution
steps.instruction: Prepare 0.05 M Fe(II) solution according to NOAA: dissolve 7.5 g iron(II) sulfate heptahydrate and add 3 mL concentrated H₂SO₄ to 500 mL ultra‑pure water and mix thoroughly.

steps.title: Add oxidation reagents and control temperature
steps.instruction: To each beaker add 50 mL of the Fe(II) solution, 50 mL of 30 % H₂O₂ and 50 mL ultra‑pure water. For compost samples add H₂O₂ slowly in increments, adding extra ultra‑pure water if foaming occurs. Monitor the temperature for the next hour and keep it ≤ 45 °C (no ice bath required).

steps.title: Initial digestion at room temperature
steps.instruction: Leave the mixtures at room temperature for 4–6 h.

steps.title: Hotplate digestion overnight
steps.instruction: Place the beakers on a hotplate set to 35 °C and leave overnight. Do not place on the hotplate earlier than this, as rapid temperature rise can cause foaming.

steps.title: Add H₂O₂ and continue digestion
steps.instruction: The following morning add 20 mL of 30 % H₂O₂ to each digest and raise the hotplate temperature to 40 °C. Add further H₂O₂ twice daily until the digest is complete.

steps.title: Terminate digestion and dilute
steps.instruction: When digestion is complete (all organic material settled, solution non‑turbid, no bubbles on gentle movement) add approximately 200 mL ultra‑pure water to each beaker to dilute residual H₂O₂. Digestion may take 2–10 days depending on sample type (soils fastest, compost and biosolids slower).

steps.title: Transfer to SMI unit and first density separation
steps.instruction: Cool the digests to room temperature, then transfer all contents to the modified SMI unit using an LDPE squeeze bottle, rinsing the beaker at least five times with ultra‑pure water. Add ultra‑pure water so the liquid level is well above the valve but ≤ 30 mm below the opening. Stir with a glass rod, rinse the rod into the unit, cover the opening with aluminium foil and let settle overnight with the valve open, rotating the valve periodically to release material from the top. The next morning close the valve, decant the supernatant and filter it onto a GF/C filter under vacuum. Rinse the SMI unit at least five times with ultra‑pure water, rinse the filtration apparatus, dry the filter under vacuum, and store it in a covered PS petri dish until analysis.

steps.title: Second density separation with NaI
steps.instruction: Open the SMI valve and add a volume equal to the bottom half of the unit (≈ 340 mL) of saturated NaI (density 3.6 g cm⁻³). Stir with a glass rod, rinsing the rod sparingly with ultra‑pure water to minimise dilution. Mixing dilutes the NaI to an approximate density of 1.8 g cm⁻³. Cover the opening with aluminium foil and let settle overnight. Close the valve, decant the supernatant and filter it onto a new GF/C filter under vacuum. Discard the remaining solution and settled solids in the bottom section.

steps.title: Filter analysis and recovery calculation
steps.instruction: Examine each filter under a Nikon SMZ1270 stereomicroscope (12.7× magnification) and count the recovered spiked particles. Calculate recovery as (recovered / spiked) × 100 %. Reported average recoveries were 92 % (compost), 95 % (biosolids) and 98 % (soil); fibre recoveries were lower (≈ 83 % compost, 90 % biosolids) due to particulate interference. Controls showed no contaminants. Transfer suspected microplastics with tweezers onto an IR‑compatible membrane (e.g., Al₂O₃) for µ‑FTIR analysis.
